annotationContent.heading: The Pattern Behind the Projects
paragraphs: Six years of work reveals a progression: from manual data analysis to scripted automation to AI-native development. Each stage wasn't just about completing projects—it was about understanding how computational intelligence changes what's possible.

At Boston Consulting Group, the initial challenge was extracting signal from massive legal datasets of inconsistent quality. Started with SQL queries and manual validation. Tedious work revealed patterns: most errors were predictable, most analysis repeatable. This led to Python scripts, then my first real AI applications. Not complex models—targeted automation that understood which patterns lawyers actually needed. Case preparation reduced from weeks to hours.

The constraint forced clarity: AI isn't magic, it's a tool with specific strengths. Instant access to domain knowledge. Pattern recognition across datasets humans can't process. No forgetting. The breakthrough was understanding these aren't incremental improvements—they represent a fundamentally different approach to knowledge work.

Founding Dormezy shifted context entirely. No established systems to optimize. Building a platform from scratch meant every architectural decision had direct consequences. The $30,000 in funding and WebSummit selection validated the approach, but the real learning came from working with developers. Their inefficiency—exploiting technical opacity, artificial delays, vendor lock-in—revealed an opportunity.

This led to committing fully to AI development. Not as an assistant but as primary builder. The progression through four generations of development approach tells the story: Week-long projects with expensive API calls became 1-2 day deliveries through spec-driven development. Each rebuild taught something new about AI's actual capabilities versus its marketed promises.

Generation 1: One week per project, Cursor with agent mode, expensive and manual. Generation 2: Five days, VS Code with Claude CLI, still heavily monitored. Generation 3: Two to three days, extensive upfront planning, manual database architecture. Generation 4: One to two days, spec-driven development, execution becomes background task.

The critical insight: AI development isn't about the tools—it's about understanding what to specify. Learned spec-driven development from first principles before discovering it had a name. The limitation isn't AI's capability but our ability to articulate requirements precisely.

Recent client work applies these lessons systematically. ApplyVisa: 40,000 programs indexed at zero external cost versus $50,000 quotes. EnglishUnleashed: 600,000 users in four months by understanding what AI voices actually optimize for (clarity for learners, not entertainment). Each project built with AI, but more importantly, built with understanding of how AI changes the economics.

This isn't a portfolio of disconnected achievements. It's documentation of learning how neural networks fundamentally alter the constraints we've built our systems around. From consulting's pattern recognition to startup's architectural decisions to current development practice—each layer compounds into capability to identify where AI creates actual leverage, not just marginal improvement.

annotationContent.heading: Application as the Final Frontier
paragraphs: Neural networks represent a fundamentally different epistemology—instant access to all domain knowledge, no forgetting, pattern recognition across infinite data points. The constraint is no longer knowledge acquisition. It's application.

Most organizations treat AI as a faster calculator, integrating it into legacy systems built on human constraints. This is like using jet engines to pull carriages. The real opportunity lies in systems designed around AI's capabilities from inception.

Products built AI-native operate on entirely different economics. When labor costs approach zero through automation, when design happens through photogrammetry, when specification generates implementation—market dynamics that seemed permanent suddenly collapse. Carvenc demonstrates this: $80,000 manual stone carving becomes $6,000 CNC fabrication. Not an improvement. A paradigm shift.

Albania's position is uniquely advantageous. No entrenched digital monopolies protecting outdated approaches. No legacy infrastructure requiring expensive retrofitting. Current digitization efforts can incorporate AI from the ground up, creating inherently superior results without fighting vestigial pre-AI redundancies.

Consider Epic in US healthcare—a universally despised monopoly that actively blocks innovation because their business model depends on complexity. Starting fresh with AI-native architecture produces solutions so superior they don't require argument. They demonstrate themselves.

Each prototype here exploits a specific constraint that AI removes. Agora: observation doesn't scale for humans but does for AI, making credentials obsolete. Hitch: pattern learning beats central planning when you can process all movement data simultaneously. These aren't features added to existing systems—they're systems that couldn't exist without AI.

The compounding advantage of AI-native development: immediate utility plus data generation that falls entirely outside existing knowledge bases. Each deployment creates scenarios that have never been implemented before, generating insights that inform more applicable AI. Legacy integrations can't replicate this feedback loop.

Application is where theory meets reality. Where 'AI can do X' becomes 'here's X creating value.' The organizations that win won't be those with the best models—they'll be those who understand how to apply the paradigm shift to create solutions impossible under previous constraints.
